$comment: Teaching content for cl_managed. Bonus material from Claude Platform 101, folded in because managed agents are the hosted form of the agent loop the exam's Domain 1 is about.

knowledgePoints.name: The loop, hosted
knowledgePoints.teach:
Managed agents are a suite of APIs for building and deploying agents at scale on Anthropic's infrastructure instead of your own server.

You define an agent — tools, persona, capabilities — configure a sandbox environment, and fire off sessions from your app. Claude runs the agent loop inside an isolated container with file system access, bash execution and web search, and you stream events back out.

You send events in and read events out. There is no manual while loop.

It is enabled by default for every API account — not a separate product to buy or a preview to request.

questions.q: What replaces the while loop when using managed agents?
options: A callback you register with the SDK
An event stream — events in, events out
A polling endpoint you check regularly
Nothing; the loop just runs remotely
questions.explain: The loop runs inside the session. Your app's relationship to it is a stream of events.

questions.q: How do you get access to managed agents?
options: Request access through the Console first
They require an enterprise agreement first
Enabled by default on every API account
Only available via Bedrock and Vertex

knowledgePoints.name: Three conditions
knowledgePoints.teach:
Reach for managed agents when the loop would:

  • run too long — minutes or hours,
  • touch too many files or tools,
  • need to survive a network hiccup — that is, need resumability.

Reach for a manual loop when you want full control.

Notice that all three conditions are about operational difficulty, not about the task being intellectually harder. A two-hour migration and a two-second lookup can be the same agent design; only one of them cares whether your process stays up for the duration.

Sessions can also run in parallel — many tickets or tasks at once, each in its own container.

questions.q: A migration agent runs for two hours across hundreds of files and must survive a dropped connection. Managed or manual?
options: Manual — you need control over a task this long
Manual, with a resume token you implement
Managed — long-running, many files, resumable
Either; the choice here is about cost alone
questions.explain: All three conditions at once. Resumability in particular is expensive to build and free here.

questions.q: When is a manual loop still the right choice?
options: When the task needs no tools of any kind
When the agent must run in your region
When the conversation exceeds the window
When you want full control of the loop
questions.explain: Control is what you give up by hosting, and it is the stated reason to keep the loop yourself.

reviewQuestions.q: What does the container an agent runs in provide?
options: File system, bash execution, and web search
A GPU for running inference locally
A persistent database for the agent
Direct access to your production network
reviewQuestions.explain: An isolated sandbox with the tools an agent typically needs — and isolation is the point of it.

knowledgePoints.name: Four things, in order
knowledgePoints.teach:
#PrimitiveWhat it is
1Agentthe persona: model, system prompt, toolset. Reusable across many runs.
2Environmentwhere it runs: cloud or local, networking config
3Sessiona single run of an agent inside an environment. The unit of work.
4Eventsmessages flowing in and out: actions, tool calls, results, replies

Agent is reusable. Session is one run. Those two are the pair most often confused.

The flow: your app talks to a session → the session drives work inside the environment → everything comes back out through the event stream.

questions.q: Which primitive is reusable across many runs, and which is a single run?
options: Session is reusable; agent is one run
Environment is reusable; agent is one run
Agent is reusable; session is one run
Both the agent and session are reusable
questions.explain: The agent is the persona you define once. Each session is one run of it.

questions.q: Which primitive is described as the unit of work?
options: Session
Agent
Environment
Event
questions.explain: A session is one run of one agent in one environment — the thing you start, track, and finish.

reviewQuestions.q: What does the environment primitive hold?
options: The system prompt and the agent toolset
Where it runs, plus its networking config
The complete event history for that run
The rubric that the output is graded on
reviewQuestions.explain: Location and networking. Persona lives on the agent.

reviewQuestions.q: Name the four primitives in order.
options: Environment, agent, session, events
Agent, session, environment, events
Session, agent, environment, events
Agent, environment, session, events
reviewQuestions.explain: Agent, environment, session, events — which is also the order you create them in.

knowledgePoints.name: Five steps, one of them a trap
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Create the agent — client.beta.agents.create(name, model, system, tools=[...]). The bundled agent toolset gives file, bash and web tools without writing your own.
  2. Create the environment — client.beta.environments.create(name, config={"type": "cloud", "networking": {...}}).
  3. Create the session — client.beta.sessions.create(agent=agent.id, environment_id=env.id, title=...).
  4. Open the event stream FIRST, then send the kickoff message.
  5. Consume the stream.

The stream only delivers events that occur after it opens. Send the kickoff first and you miss the beginning of your own run.

The failure is confusing precisely because the agent works: it runs correctly, does the job, and your application simply never saw the first few events. Watch for agent.message (Claude's text), agent.tool_use (which tool it picked) and session.status_idle (it is done).

questions.q: Your managed agent runs correctly but your app sees none of the first few events. What did you get wrong?
options: You sent the kickoff before opening the stream
You created the session before the environment
You did not subscribe to agent.tool_use events
You polled the session instead of streaming
questions.explain: The stream only delivers what happens after it opens. Open first, then kick off.

questions.q: Which event tells you the agent has finished?
options: agent.message
agent.tool_use
session.complete
session.status_idle
questions.explain: session.status_idle — the agent has nothing left to do.

reviewQuestions.q: What does the bundled agent toolset provide?
options: File, bash and web tools, ready-made
A set of MCP server connections to use
Pre-built rubrics and output graders
Client-side schemas for your functions
reviewQuestions.explain: The common agent tools, ready-made — which is what makes the smallest managed agent genuinely small.

reviewQuestions.q: Which event carries the name of the tool the agent picked?
options: agent.message
agent.tool_use
session.status_idle
agent.action

knowledgePoints.name: What turns a demo into an operation
knowledgePoints.teach:
Building blockWhat it gives you
Rubrics & graderssuccess criteria, plus a grader with its own context window that evaluates output against them; Claude iterates until it passes
Memoryread a store before starting, write when done — cross-session continuity, so it knows prices are 15% lower than last week rather than repeating a stale figure
Multi-agent coordinationa coordinator delegates to specialists, each in its own context window over a shared file system; the coordinator synthesises their findings
Permissions policiessensitive actions — posting to Slack, say — pause for human approval before executing

The grader gets its own context window so it judges the output, not the reasoning that produced it.

A grader sharing the producer's context has already been persuaded — it saw every justification along the way. Isolation is what makes the grade independent.

questions.q: Your managed agent must never post to Slack without sign-off, and must remember last week's prices. Which two building blocks?
options: Rubrics and multi-agent coordination
Memory and rubrics used together
Permissions and multi-agent coordination
Permissions policies plus memory
questions.explain: A permissions policy pauses the sensitive action; memory carries knowledge across sessions.

questions.q: Why does a grader get its own context window?
options: To keep the producer's context small
Because graders run on a different tier
So it judges independently of the reasoning
To allow the grade itself to be cached
questions.explain: Independence. A grader that saw every justification has already been argued into agreement.

reviewQuestions.q: In managed multi-agent coordination, how do specialists share their work?
options: Through a single shared context window
Over a shared file system the coordinator reads
By passing messages directly to each other
Through a shared memory store, and only that
reviewQuestions.explain: Own context windows, shared file system, coordinator synthesises — hub-and-spoke, with the file system as the medium.

reviewQuestions.q: Can managed sessions run in parallel?
options: No — only one session per agent at a time
Only within one and the same environment
Only for the agents that are read-only
Yes — many at once, each in its container
reviewQuestions.explain: Parallel sessions, isolated containers — which is much of the point of hosting them.
